FIRST WARN FORECAST
Monday, September 7, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

HAPPY LABOR DAY AND HAPPY BIRTHDAY, DR. NICK!

After nearly a week of dangerous late-summer heat, Labor Day finally brings a noticeable change in the weather pattern. Cooler temperatures, lower humidity and a much more comfortable air mass will dominate today before summer makes a brief return Tuesday and Wednesday. Today will be the most comfortable day we have experienced in quite some time, with afternoon temperatures generally in the mid-80s to around 90 degrees and dewpoints falling into the 50s and lower 60s. The difference in humidity will be especially noticeable compared with the oppressive conditions of the past week.

A persistent northeast to east wind will continue pulling cooler and drier air into Missouri and Illinois today. That will keep afternoon temperatures much more manageable, while the lower humidity will make it feel even more comfortable. Tonight, temperatures will fall into the 60s across most of the region, with some sheltered locations in southeastern and east-central Missouri and southwestern Illinois potentially dropping into the upper 50s. For those with outdoor plans today, the weather should cooperate nicely. After the heat we have endured, this is the kind of September weather that feels especially welcome.

Unfortunately, the cooler weather will not last long. The upper-level ridge that has dominated our weather pattern will begin shifting eastward Tuesday, allowing warmer air to return from the southwest. Temperatures will climb back into the low to mid-90s, but there is an important difference between this warmup and the heatwave we just experienced. Moisture will be slower to return, meaning humidity will remain relatively limited Tuesday and heat index values should stay much closer to actual air temperatures. It will be hot, but it should not feel nearly as oppressive.

Wednesday will be the more complicated day of the forecast. Temperatures are expected to climb into the mid to upper 90s ahead of an approaching cold front, particularly across areas south of Interstate 70. The timing of that front has been trending slightly earlier in recent forecast guidance, which introduces some uncertainty regarding just how hot Wednesday becomes. Increasing moisture near the front could push heat index values into the 100 to 105 degree range, and another Heat Advisory may eventually need to be considered for portions of the region. At this point, however, confidence is not high enough to determine whether additional heat headlines will be necessary.

The approaching cold front will also bring our next significant opportunity for rainfall. Showers and thunderstorms are expected to develop Wednesday afternoon and evening and continue into early Thursday as the front slowly advances southward. This system has a much stronger signal for rainfall than anything we have seen recently, with most forecast guidance indicating a high probability of measurable precipitation from Wednesday afternoon into Thursday morning. Some areas, particularly near the I-70 and I-44 corridors, could receive one-half inch or more of rain, although the exact placement of the heaviest rainfall will depend on how quickly the front moves through the region.

There is also a low-end severe weather threat Wednesday afternoon and evening. The atmosphere should contain enough instability and wind shear to support a few strong thunderstorms, and an isolated severe storm cannot be ruled out. However, a strong cap across the warm sector and the fact that the strongest forcing and wind shear may remain behind the surface front should limit the overall threat. At this point, I am not expecting a widespread severe weather event, but a few storms could produce strong wind gusts and locally heavy rainfall.

Thursday will bring a much cooler pattern behind the front. Showers and thunderstorms should gradually diminish from north to south Thursday morning into midday, although clouds and lingering precipitation could keep temperatures in the low to mid-80s. Parts of southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois could remain even cooler if rain and thicker cloud cover persist into the afternoon. Once the front clears the region, we should begin moving toward a drier pattern.

The forecast becomes considerably less certain heading into next weekend. Long-range computer models continue to disagree on the exact position and movement of the upper-level ridge across the country. One scenario would bring the ridge back over the Mid-Mississippi River Valley and produce another period of hot, well-above-average temperatures. Another keeps the ridge farther west or southwest, which would leave us with temperatures only modestly above normal. Either scenario could also produce occasional opportunities for showers and thunderstorms as disturbances move around the ridge, but the overall pattern currently favors more dry weather than wet weather.

The bottom line is that Labor Day provides a much-needed break from the extreme heat, with comfortable temperatures and significantly lower humidity today. Summer returns briefly Tuesday and Wednesday, but this next warmup appears likely to be shorter and less oppressive than the heatwave we just experienced. Wednesday will bring the next significant weather system, with a cold front, widespread opportunities for showers and thunderstorms, and a limited threat for a few strong storms. Cooler weather follows Thursday, although the longer-range forecast remains uncertain.

For now, enjoy Labor Day. After nearly a week of oppressive heat, a cool breeze and lower humidity are certainly worth appreciating. And yes, today happens to be my birthday, too. I cannot think of a better birthday present from Mother Nature than a forecast that finally gives us a chance to get outside and enjoy the day.

Happy Labor Day, everyone, and thank you for spending another year of weather with me.

Dr. Nick

First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
